messages.subject: Growth Mixture model
parts:
Dear all,
I have fitted a growth mixture model (with two latent classes) in Rjags, (The syntax are as follow). I am wounding how can I fit this model in Rstan. Specially, how do you specify "latent class indicator" in Rstan? 
Here I have defined a logistic regression for latent-class specification. (showed in red color) . I do have difficulty with this part in R-satn. (R-stan syntax are presented in below)

Thanks in advance for any help!

Kazem

## Syntax in R-jags
model {   
for(j in 1:n) {
for(i in offset[j]:(offset[j+1]-1)){
Hb[i]~dnorm(mu[i],tau)
mu[i]<-beta[1]*Age[j]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+beta[4]*TSPD2[i]+beta[5]*(1-d[i])+
equals(g[j],1)*(theta1[1]+b01[j])+ # 1st calss 
equals(g[j],2)*(theta2[1]+b02[j,1]+d[i]*(theta2[2]+b02[j,2])*TD[i]+d[i]*(theta2[3])*TD2[i])# 2nd calss  
 }
b01[j]~dnorm(0,taub)
b02[j,1:2]~dmnorm(mub,Omega2[,])
g[j] ~ dcat(psi[j,])        # Latent class indicator
psi[j,1] <- 1 - psi[j,2] 
logit(psi[j,2]) <- gamma[1]+ gamma[2]*Age[j]+gamma[3]*Hb0[j]
}
Omega2[1:2,1:2]~dwish(R,2)
sigmab2[1:2,1:2]<-inverse(Omega2[,])
taub~dgamma(0.01,0.01)
sigmab<-1/taub
sigmab1<-sqrt(sigmab)
tau~dgamma(0.01,0.01)
sigma2<-1/tau
sigma<-sqrt(sigma2)
for(k in 1:5) {
beta[k]~dnorm(0,0.01)
}
theta2[1]~dnorm(0,0.01)
theta2[2]~dnorm(0,0.01)I(,0)
theta2[3]~dnorm(0,0.01)
theta1~dnorm(0,0.01)
## Priors for class parameters
for(c2 in 1:3) {gamma[c2]~dnorm(0,0.0001)}
}
###
### Syntax in R-Stan
data {
int<lower=1> n ;
int<lower=1> ntot ;
int<lower=1> offset ;
int <lower=0, upper=1> d[ntot] ;
real Hb[ntot] ;
real Hb0[n] ;
real Age[n] ;
int <lower=0,upper=1> Season[ntot] ;
int <lower=0> TSPD[ntot] ;
int <lower=0> TSPD2[ntot] ;
int <lower=0> TD[ntot] ;
int <lower=0> TD2[ntot] ;
cov_matrix[2] Rb;
vector[2] mub; 
}

parameters {
cov_matrix[2] sigma2b;
vector[1] theta1 ;
vector[3] theta2 ;
vector[1] b01[n] ;
vector[2] b02[n] ;
real<lower=0,upper=20> sigma;
real<lower=0,upper=20> sigmab1;
vector[1] g[n];
vector[5] beta;
vector[3] gamma;
}

model {
sigma2b~inv_wishart(2,Rb);
for (j in 1:n) {
b01[j]~normal(0,sigmab1);
b02[j]~multi_normal(mub,sigma2b);
g[j]~bernoulli(exp(gamma[1]+gamma[2]*Age[j]+gamma[3]*Hb0[j])/(1+exp(gamma[1]+gamma[2]*Age[j]+gamma[3]*Hb0[j])));
}
for(j in 1:n) {
for(i in offset[j]:(offset[j+1]-1)){
Hb[i] ~  normal(beta[1]*Age[j]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+beta[4]*TSPD2[i]+beta[5]*(1-d[i])+
operator==(g[j],0)*(theta1[1]+b01[j])+ // 1st calss 
operator==(g[j],1)*(theta2[1]+b02[j,1]+d[i]*(theta2[2]+b02[j,2])*TD[i]+d[i]*(theta2[3])*TD2[i])// 2nd calss
,sigma);
}
}
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Growth Mixture model
parts:
The problem you're having is that Stan doesn't support integer parameters,
and if you try to declare g as real as you do, it won't match the Bernoulli
distribution's outcome type, which is int.

You need to marginalize out any discrete parameters in a Stan model.
There's a chapter in the manual on mixture modeling. It's a pain from the
coding side, but the upside is that it runs much much faster than sampling
the discrete parameters.

In your case, Hb[i] should be drawn from a mixture of normals
with mixing proportions equal to psi[j]. It looks like there
are only two cases g[j] == 1 and g[j] == 2, so it should be
relatively straightforward (i.e., you won't need intermediate
variables or a loop). And given thatit's binary, it's probably
easy to use a Bernoulli structure rather than a categorical.

See below for where this has to be done.

I'd also suggest starting with simpler models and working up.
Start with simpler priors, fewer effects, etc. It's much easier
to code that way than starting with a big model and trying to
debug it.

- Bob

Thanks Bob for your valuable help.
I have already fitted a mixture model with 4 latent classes. It works well!!! 
The syntax for a simple model without random effects in the model are as below:
Now I have some more questions: (Please look at below)

########## Stan syntax
data {
  int k ;                           // Number of latent class
  int ntot ;    // Number of Observations
  real Age[ntot] ;
  int n ;                          // Number of individuals
  int<lower=1> offset[51];
  real <lower=0,upper=1> Season[ntot] ;
  real <lower=0> TSPD[ntot] ;
  real Hb[ntot];
 }

parameters {
  
  simplex[k] pi[n]; //mixing proportions
  
  real<lower=0,upper=1> sigma; //scale parameters of mixture components
  
  vector[k] theta1;          // Non-shared parameter

  vector[3] beta; // Shared parameters
}

model {
  real psi[k];
  beta~normal(0,1);
  theta1~normal(9,1)T[0,];

for(j in 1:n) {
    
  for(i in offset[j]:(offset[j+1]-1)){

psi[1]<- log(pi[j,1])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[1], sigma);
  psi[2]<- log(pi[j,2])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[2], sigma);
  psi[3]<- log(pi[j,3])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[3], sigma);
  psi[4]<- log(pi[j,4])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[4], sigma);
      
   increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(psi));
      
    }
}    

}
####

Since in Stan the discrete distributions for the parameters are not possible, how can you define a distribution for the pi[j,c] (j=1,2,....,n), (c=1,2,3,4) that is probability for the person j belong to class c in above syntax? (In rjags, I used below codes). Finally to identify gamma's in the below model, we have to constrain one of the classes's gammas to zero. How can we constrain a parameter to zero (or other values in Stan)?
e.g., 
gamma[1,1]<-0
gamma[1,2]<-0
gamma[1,3]<-0


A part of syntax for rjags
################
g[j] ~ dcat(psi[j,]) # Latent class indicator

for(c in 1:4)
{
psi[j,c]<-phi[j,c]/sum(phi[j,])
log(phi[j,c])<-gamma[c,1]+ gamma[c,2]*Age0[j]+gamma[c,3]*Hb0[j]
}
}
##########

Thanks so much in advance for spending time to answer the questions.
Kazem

>
> psi[1]<- log(pi[j,1])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[1], sigma);
> psi[2]<- log(pi[j,2])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[2], sigma);
> psi[3]<- log(pi[j,3])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[3], sigma);
> psi[4]<- log(pi[j,4])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[4], sigma);
>
> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(psi));
>
> }
> }

Given the truncation on theta1, you need to define it as:

vector<lower=0>[k] theta1;

Once you do that, because it's given a normal(9,1) distribution,
it doesn't need the truncation (it's implicit in the declaration),
so you can more efficiently write:

theta1 ~ normal(9,1);

We usually follow the convention of capitalizing size constants.

Is there a reason to bound sigma above at 1?

> Since in Stan the discrete distributions for the parameters are not possible, how can you define a distribution for the pi[j,c] (j=1,2,....,n), (c=1,2,3,4) that is probability for the person j belong to class c in above syntax? (In rjags, I used below codes).

I'm not sure what you mean here. The pi as you wrote it in the above model
gets a uniform distribution over simplexes (that's proper because they're
bounded). You can do inference using just the pi --- you don't need the
indicator variable g. The normalization is done through the simplex definition.

Did you want to add some other kind of prior?

> Finally to identify gamma's in the below model, we have to constrain one of the classes's gammas to zero. How can we constrain a parameter to zero (or other values in Stan)?
> e.g.,
> gamma[1,1]<-0
> gamma[1,2]<-0
> gamma[1,3]<-0

You don't need to do this to identify in Stan. It's implicit
in the way the simplex is defined. What happens is that your
pi is a 4-simplex from the model's perspective, but is underlyingly
parameterized using 3 free parameters, so there's no problem with
identification of pi itself.

As with any mixture model, the indexes won't be clearly defined,
but there's not much we can do about that --- there's a discussion
in the manual in the problematic posteriors chapter.

>
>
> A part of syntax for rjags
> ################
> g[j] ~ dcat(psi[j,]) # Latent class indicator
>
> for(c in 1:4)
> {
> psi[j,c]<-phi[j,c]/sum(phi[j,])
> log(phi[j,c])<-gamma[c,1]+ gamma[c,2]*Age0[j]+gamma[c,3]*Hb0[j]
> }
> }
> ##########

Usually more is better than less here --- doesn't phi here
need to be given some kind of prior?

- Bob

Regarding to your reply,
Sorry if the question was not obvious, I explain it again in below:

In the current model we assumed the pi[j,c] comes from a simplex distribution that I think is similar to rjags when we assume pi[j,] ~ ddirch(1,1,1,1). (Let's call this model A.)

But I am going to define a model for pi[j,c] (class probability for each individual) as well based on some other covariates (e.g., Age and Hb at baseline) and put priors for these parameters. (Let's call this model B.)

Please see in below the two models in rjags. I am interested in model B in Rstan.

   for(j in 1:n) {
g[j] ~ dcat(psi[j,]) # Latent class indicator

pi[j,1:4]<-ddirch(1,1,1,1)
 } 
 

##########

g[j] ~ dcat(psi[j,]) # Latent class indicator

Given the truncation on theta1, you need to define it as:

   vector<lower=0>[k] theta1;

Once you do that, because it's given a normal(9,1) distribution,
it doesn't need the truncation (it's implicit in the declaration),
so you can more efficiently write:

  theta1 ~ normal(9,1);

We usually follow the convention of capitalizing size constants.

Is there a reason to bound sigma above at 1?  


> Since in Stan the discrete distributions for the parameters are not possible, how can you define a distribution for the pi[j,c] (j=1,2,....,n), (c=1,2,3,4) that is probability for the person j belong to class c in above syntax? (In rjags, I used below codes).

I'm not sure what you mean here.  The pi as you wrote it in the above model
gets a uniform distribution over simplexes (that's proper because they're
bounded).  You can do inference using just the pi --- you don't need the
indicator variable g.  The normalization is done through the simplex definition.

Did you want to add some other kind of prior?

> Finally to identify gamma's in the below model, we have to constrain one of the classes's gammas to zero. How can we constrain a parameter to zero (or other values in Stan)?
> e.g.,
> gamma[1,1]<-0
> gamma[1,2]<-0
> gamma[1,3]<-0

You don't need to do this to identify in Stan.  It's implicit
in the way the simplex is defined.  What happens is that your
pi is a 4-simplex from the model's perspective, but is underlyingly
parameterized using 3 free parameters, so there's no problem with
identification of pi itself.

As with any mixture model, the indexes won't be clearly defined,
but there's not much we can do about that --- there's a discussion
in the manual in the problematic posteriors chapter.

Usually more is better than less here --- doesn't phi here
need to be given some kind of prior?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Growth Mixture model
parts:
On Apr 14, 2014, at 4:34 PM, Kazem <nasser...@gmail.com> wrote:

> ...

> In the current model we assumed the pi[j,c] comes from a simplex distribution that I think is similar to rjags when we assume pi[j,] ~ ddirch(1,1,1,1). (Let's call this model A.)
>
Right. It's identical in terms of distribution for pi.

> But I am going to define a model for pi[j,c] (class probability for each individual) as well based on some other covariates (e.g., Age and Hb at baseline) and put priors for these parameters. (Let's call this model B.)

> ################
> for(j in 1:n) {
> g[j] ~ dcat(psi[j,]) # Latent class indicator
>
> for(c in 1:4)
> {
> psi[j,c]<-phi[j,c]/sum(phi[j,])
> log(phi[j,c])<-gamma[c,1]+ gamma[c,2]*Age0[j]+gamma[c,3]*Hb0[j]
> }
> }
> ##########

If you transpose the gammas, you can define psi without a loop as:

psi[j] <- softmax(gamma[1] + gamma[2] * Age0[j] + gamma[3] * Hb0[j]);

The Stan notation gamma[2] is equivalent to R/JAGS/BUGS gamma[2,], and
now I'm assuming gamma is the transpose of what you have and that it's
defined as an array of vectors (or a matrix, though the array of vectors
is more efficient --- see the manual chapter on vectors vs. arrays).

But even better is to not bother with the softmax at all, and use
the logit-parameterized categorical, which would reduce all of the
above to just:

for (j in 1:n)
g[j] ~ categorical_logit(gamma[1] + gamma[2] * Age0[j] + gamma[3] * Hb0[j]);

- Bob

parts:
On Apr 14, 2014, at 6:52 PM, Kazem <nasser...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks Bob,
>
> Regarding to below model,
>
> for (j in 1:n)
> g[j] ~ categorical_logit(gamma[1] + gamma[2] * Age0[j] + gamma[3] * Hb0[j]);
>
>
> g[j] is also parameter, I think Stan can not handle this (because it is a discreet parameter), right? I think I have to write a model directly for pi[j,c].

Sorry -- you're absolutely right. Stan doesn't allow discrete parameters.
So instead,
softmax(gamma[1] + gamma[2] * Age0[j] + gamma[3] * Hb0[j])

will give you the distribution over g on the linear scale. You'll then
have to use that as in other mixture models for whatever you would've used
g for, but it looks like you had that sorted in the previous models.

- Bob
